title: Bastante vs Suficiente: Enough, Quite or Rather?
seo_title: Bastante vs Suficiente: Enough, Quite or Rather?
meta_description: Bastante vs suficiente: both can mean enough, but bastante also means quite. Learn when to use each, how they agree, and lo suficientemente, with a quiz.
excerpt: Two words for “enough”, one of which also means “quite”. Here is how to tell them apart.

body_html:
Bastante vs suficiente confuses learners because both words can translate as “enough”. The difference: suficiente means exactly enough, no more and no less, while bastante usually means “quite” or “quite a lot”, and only sometimes “enough”. Es bastante caro means “it’s quite expensive”, not “it’s expensive enough”. If you want to say something is big enough, you need lo suficientemente grande.

Quick answer
  • Suficiente = enough, sufficient: No tenemos suficientes sillas.
  • Bastante before an adjective = quite, rather: Es bastante difícil.
  • Bastante with a noun = quite a lot of, or enough: Hay bastante gente.
  • “Adjective + enough” is lo suficientemente + adjective: lo suficientemente alto.
{{toc}}

Bastante vs suficiente: the core difference

SuficienteBastante
Main meaningEnough, as much as neededQuite, rather, a fair amount
With a nounsuficiente dinero enough moneybastante dinero quite a lot of money
With an adjectivelo suficientemente rápido fast enoughbastante rápido quite fast
AloneEs suficiente. That’s enough.Ya tengo bastante. I have plenty already.

The easiest way to remember it: suficiente measures against a need, bastante measures against what you expected.

How to use suficiente

Suficiente works like the English “enough” or “sufficient”. It agrees in number with the noun but not in gender:

  • ¿Tienes suficiente tiempo? Do you have enough time?
  • No hay suficientes platos para todos. There aren’t enough plates for everyone.
  • Con dos horas es suficiente. Two hours is enough.
  • Ya fue suficiente. That’s enough now. (to stop an argument or a behavior)

When “enough” follows an adjective or adverb in English, Spanish uses lo suficientemente before it: No es lo suficientemente grande (It isn’t big enough). Corre lo suficientemente rápido (He runs fast enough).

{{image:2}}

How to use bastante

Bastante has two jobs. Before adjectives and adverbs, it is an adverb meaning “quite” or “rather”, and it never changes form:

  • La película fue bastante buena. The movie was pretty good.
  • Habla inglés bastante bien. She speaks English quite well.
  • Las tortillas están bastante calientes. The tortillas are quite hot.

With nouns, it means “quite a lot of” or “enough”, and it agrees in number: Tengo bastantes amigos aquí (I have quite a few friends here). Ya comí bastante (I’ve eaten plenty).

Context decides whether it sounds like “enough” or “a lot”. Tenemos bastante comida at a party usually means “we have plenty”, which is close to “enough”.

Basta and ya basta

Both words come from the verb bastar, to be enough. You will hear it most in ¡Basta! or ¡Ya basta!, “That’s enough!”, said to children, in an argument or at a protest. It is strong, so use it carefully.

A softer everyday phrase is Con eso basta (That will do) or Basta con… (It’s enough to…): Basta con llamar un día antes (Just call a day before).

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Why bastante vs suficiente is tricky

English “enough” always measures against a need. Spanish splits that job, and bastante drifts toward a different meaning altogether. Learners who translate “quite” as muy and “enough” as bastante end up saying things they don’t mean: El examen fue bastante fácil sounds like “the exam was quite easy”, which may or may not be what you want to say.

Tone matters too. Bastante before an adjective often softens a judgment, much like “pretty” in American English: Está bastante bien (It’s pretty good). People use it to be polite when something is fine but not amazing.

Practice sentences

Translate these, then check your answers below.

  1. Do we have enough chairs?
  2. The hotel was pretty expensive.
  3. He isn’t old enough to drive.
  4. I’ve had plenty, thanks.

Answers: 1. ¿Tenemos suficientes sillas? 2. El hotel fue bastante caro. 3. No tiene la edad suficiente para manejar or No es lo suficientemente mayor para manejar. 4. Ya comí bastante, gracias.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • No es suficiente grande. “Big enough” needs lo suficientemente: No es lo suficientemente grande.
  • Son bastantes caros. As an adverb before an adjective, bastante doesn’t change: Son bastante caros.
  • Es bastante when you mean “it’s enough”. To stop someone serving you, say Es suficiente, gracias or Así está bien, gracias.
  • Tengo bastante problemas. With a plural noun: Tengo bastantes problemas.

The two words often appear together with {{link:muy-vs-mucho|muy vs mucho}}, another pair about quantity and intensity.

In real conversation

At a family dinner in Mexico, you will hear both words within a minute:

—¿Te sirvo más arroz?
—No, gracias, ya comí bastante. Estuvo bastante rico.
—¿Seguro? ¿Te alcanzó?
—Sí, de verdad, fue más que suficiente.

“More rice?” “No thanks, I’ve had plenty. It was really good.” “Are you sure? Was it enough?” “Yes, really, it was more than enough.” Notice also alcanzar, which in Mexico often means “to be enough”: No me alcanza el dinero (I don’t have enough money).

The RAE dictionary lists both meanings of bastante if you want to see more examples.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Bastante vs suficiente comes down to one question: are you measuring against what is needed, or against what you expected? Use suficiente for “enough”, bastante for “quite”, and lo suficientemente before adjectives. For the other pairs learners mix up, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between bastante and suficiente?
faq.a: Suficiente means enough or sufficient. Bastante usually means quite or quite a lot, and only sometimes enough.

faq.q: How do I say “big enough” in Spanish?
faq.a: Use lo suficientemente before the adjective: lo suficientemente grande.
Only with nouns: bastantes amigos. Before adjectives it is an adverb and stays the same: bastante caros.
Besides “to reach”, it often means “to be enough”: ¿Te alcanza? Is it enough for you?
